title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI can function as a teaching partner in K-12 classrooms, focusing on how teacher-facing and student-facing AI tools are designed, implemented, and perceived during classroom codesign. The central question is not a head-to-head efficacy comparison with a human coach, but rather how AI-supported features can extend instruction, provide formative feedback, and help teachers manage planning, assessment, and student inquiry while preserving teacher judgment.

The pilot introduced four Colleague AI Classroom features: Teaching Aide for structured student-AI conversations, Assessment and AI Grading for rubric generation and formative feedback, AI Tutor for student self-directed support, and Student Growth Insights for teacher-facing summaries of student thinking. The study ran for seven weeks in spring 2025 with 21 in-service teachers from Washington State districts and one independent school, serving more than 600 students in grades 6-12. Teachers planned AI-integrated lessons, implemented them in live classrooms, and provided surveys, reflections, meetings, and interviews; platform logs were also analyzed.

Findings suggest that AI was most useful when tightly scaffolded by teachers through clear prompts, goals, rubrics, and monitoring. Teachers valued narrative feedback more than numeric scores, used AI outputs as first-pass formative scaffolds, and relied on teacher oversight to maintain trust and contextualize results. Student engagement and learning were strongest when activities were aligned to instructional goals and developmentally appropriate, while implementation was more mixed in subjects requiring precise reasoning or diagram-based work. Overall, the study concludes that generative AI can augment classroom instruction as a collaborative “third agent,” but its effectiveness depends heavily on teacher AI competency, framing, and human oversight.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, formative pilot with surveys, logs, interviews, and teacher reflections, not a controlled impact study. It provides useful implementation evidence, but the paper explicitly notes reliance on self-report and the absence of direct student outcome measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests promising but unquantified benefits for feedback speed, engagement, and some subject-specific learning, with no standardized effect sizes reported. Because the evidence is exploratory and mostly self-reported, impact is modest and unclear rather than demonstrably large.

interventions.use_case: teacher-authored, teacher-supervised student-AI conversations for class discussion, inquiry, seminar prep, and guided independent tutoring via Teaching Aide and AI Tutor
automated rubric generation, AI-assisted grading, and narrative formative feedback on student work with teacher review and final grading authority
Student Growth Insights that aggregates student-AI interaction logs to surface common questions, misconceptions, and growth patterns for teachers to guide reteaching and instructional adjustment

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI grading and Student Growth Insights reduced time spent on feedback and scanning student work. In the assessment module, median AI grading coverage reached 92.2% across 58 assessments, and teachers described the system as a helpful first-pass feedback engine that sped turnaround and reduced burden; SGI was also described as saving hours of scanning and helping with targeted reteaching.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of feedback usefulness, grading coverage in platform logs, and self-reported time saved on scanning/feedback
finding.study_size: n=19 teachers for assessment implementation; 58 assessments across 33 classrooms; 936 student submissions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that immediate AI feedback and low-pressure AI conversations sometimes increased student confidence, engagement, and willingness to participate, especially for multilingual learners or anxious students. However, engagement was uneven across classes and some students were overwhelmed by long responses or disengaged when teacher framing was weak.
finding.measure: Teacher exit tickets and surveys on engagement, learning, and confidence; reported student participation patterns
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide; n=13 teachers for assessment feedback survey

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests AI-supported activities could prompt deeper inquiry, revision, and evidence-based reasoning when teachers provided strong scaffolds and clear goals. At the same time, teachers noted shallow exchanges, off-task dialogue, and overreliance risks, so gains in critical thinking and metacognition were contingent on teacher mediation rather than the AI alone.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative reflections on inquiry depth, revision behavior, and evidence-based reasoning
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; 114 Teaching Aide conversations; 58 assessments

finding.finding_summary: In ELA and Spanish implementations, teachers reported that AI-supported prewriting, brainstorming, and proficiency feedback improved writing-related work and revision opportunities. Teachers especially valued narrative feedback for guiding student revisions, though the report does not provide standardized literacy outcome scores.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of writing quality, revision quality, and usefulness of AI feedback in ELA/Spanish tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across humanities, Spanish, and interdisciplinary STEM contexts, teachers reported that AI-assisted conversations and formative feedback could support content learning, but outcomes varied substantially by subject and task fit. The report emphasizes stronger fit in language and exploratory discussion tasks, with more mixed results in math and earth science where diagrams and technical reasoning were harder for the AI to handle.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative reports of subject-specific learning and assignment quality

finding.finding_summary: Math classrooms showed more variable results than other subjects, with some teachers noting useful concept talk and inquiry support, but others reporting frustration with Socratic style responses and difficulty handling non-linear problem solving or diagrams. The report does not provide achievement test data, only teacher-reported implementation outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative reports from middle school algebra/geometry implementations and math assessment use

finding.finding_summary: Science teachers reported that AI-assisted conversations sometimes supported inquiry and culturally relevant content, and assessment feedback could help with revision and formative learning. However, earth science and some STEM tasks were limited by diagram handling and technical reasoning challenges, yielding mixed implementation quality rather than uniform gains.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative reports of inquiry, reasoning, and subject-task fit in science classes
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers; 7 science classes in the pilot
